summary:
## Benchmark Overview
- A performance comparison of three popular Rust web frameworks: **Actix**, **Axum**, and **Rocket**.
- Applications are deployed in a **Kubernetes (EKS)** cluster on AWS `m7a.8xlarge` instances.
- Load is generated by Kubernetes jobs, gradually increasing by **1,000 requests per second** every 3 minutes.

## Key Performance Metrics
- **CPU & Memory Usage**: Measured as a percentage of the limit set in Kubernetes.
- **Client-side Latency**: The primary metric, measured using the **p99 percentile**.
- **Requests Per Second (RPS)**: The throughput of each application.
- **Availability**: Percentage of successful requests (HTTP 2xx).
- **CPU Throttling**: Monitored to see if applications hit their CPU limits.

## Application & Test Setup
- Each application exposes a single `/api/devices` endpoint that returns a hardcoded JSON payload.
- Built in **release mode** with standard Rust optimizations.
- Packaged into a minimal **distroless Debian** Docker image.
- Client timeout is set to **200 milliseconds**. Requests exceeding this time are considered failures (HTTP 408).

> [!NOTE]
> The source code is available on GitHub, and community contributions to improve the test applications are encouraged.

## Performance Analysis & Key Findings

### Low to Medium Load
- At idle, all frameworks show minimal CPU and memory usage, with **Axum** having the flattest memory profile.
- Under light load, **Rocket** exhibits higher latency and CPU usage compared to the others.
- **Actix** and **Axum** perform almost identically under light load (up to ~20% of max).
- As load increases to ~30%, differences become more apparent: **Actix** shows the lowest latency, followed by **Axum**, then **Rocket**.

### High Load & Breaking Point
- Application **failure** is defined by availability dropping due to client timeouts (requests > 200ms), not by hitting 100% CPU or memory.
- All three frameworks started to fail at approximately **27,000 requests per second**.
- The maximum sustainable load before significant performance degradation was around **26,000 RPS**.

### Final Results
- **CPU Usage**: `Rocket > Axum > Actix`. **Actix** was the most CPU-efficient.
- **Latency**: `Rocket > Axum > Actix`. **Actix** consistently had the lowest latency across all load levels.
- **Availability**: Although all failed around the same load, **Actix** showed slightly higher availability, serving more successful requests before failing.
- **Memory**: Memory usage remained steady for all frameworks until they approached their breaking point, at which point it spiked due to queuing pending requests.
- **CPU Throttling**: No CPU throttling occurred for any application.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Actix** emerged as the top performer in this specific benchmark, demonstrating the lowest latency and CPU usage while maintaining high availability up to the breaking point.
transcription:
## Introduction to the Rust Framework Benchmark

In this short video, we’ll compare one of the most popular Rust frameworks. I’ll deploy all three applications to Kubernetes, and we’ll use Prometheus and Grafana to monitor them. We’ll measure the CPU usage of each application relative to the limit set in the Kubernetes deployment. Memory usage will also be measured relative to its limit. You could measure actual values, like how many megabytes or gigabytes of memory the application uses, but it’s much easier to set up alarms based on usage percentage thresholds.

We’ll also measure how many requests each application can process, as well as, most importantly, the client-side latency—how long it takes to process each request. We’ll use the p99 percentile for this measurement. I explained how percentiles work in this video.

We’ll also measure the availability of each application, which is the number of successful requests divided by the total requests, then multiplied by 100. Finally, since we are running these applications in Kubernetes, we need to measure CPU throttling as well.

## Test Environment and Application Overview

I’ve created a production-ready EKS cluster in AWS to run each test. If you’re interested, I have a full course on my channel on how to create one. I’m using the new m7a.8xlarge instances. The applications I’m testing only get a subset of the available CPU and memory, while the rest is reserved for other infrastructure and clients generating load.

Each application has an /api/devices endpoint that returns the data to the client in JSON format. You can find the source code in my public GitHub repo. If you think anything can be improved, any tips or pull requests are always welcome. If the changes make a difference, I will update the video with the new results.

Each application also includes standard Rust optimizations for the release profile. All of them are built with the release flag, and I used a distroless Debian image to create the Docker images.

If you're curious, here are the final image sizes. We could reduce them even further by using UPX, as I did with Go images, bringing them down to 3 or 4 megabytes. However, for this test, the size doesn't really matter.

## Idle State & Initial Load Test Analysis

Alright, let’s deploy all three applications to Kubernetes and maybe run them for 15 minutes in an idle state. You can see a slight difference in CPU usage between the frameworks, but it's really, really small and doesn’t mean much at this point. On the other hand, memory usage is also very small, but you may notice a different behavior. Axum shows a flat memory usage, while Actix and Rocket have some spikes.

Now, let’s start the test and deploy Kubernetes jobs to generate the load. The entire test took about 1.5 hours, but I’ve reduced it to just a few minutes for this video. And at the end, we’ll go through each graph for the entire test duration.

We’re going to gradually increase the number of virtual clients every 3 minutes by 1,000 requests per second and continue until these applications start to fail. At the start of the test, with a small load, the most important metric is client latency.

You can see that the Rocket framework, even at the beginning, has the highest latency, and its CPU usage is also higher than the other frameworks. However, memory usage remains steady for the entire duration because Rust doesn't have garbage collection, and we’re not using much memory—we're just returning hardcoded values in JSON format.

At this point, Actix and Axum have similar CPU and latency performance. This is around 20% of the maximum load these applications can handle, so we can conclude that under low load, Actix and Axum behave almost the same. However, in real-world testing, we would want to explore all possible scenarios, including pushing each application to its breaking point.

I should mention that I ran this test multiple times on different EC2 instances to ensure there were no noisy neighbors, and the results were consistent.

## Mid-Load Performance and Defining Failure

Now, let’s continue running the test for a few more minutes. At about 30% of the total requests each application can handle, we start to see differences. At 30%, which I would still consider a light load, Actix has the lowest latency, followed by Axum, with Rocket being the slowest. As we increase the load, the difference between Actix and Axum becomes more noticeable, not just in latency but also in CPU usage. Although the difference is small, it’s still apparent.

At this point, the average request takes about 100 to 200 microseconds, not milliseconds. I set the client timeout for this test to 200 milliseconds. So, when the client requests start to time out, they receive 408 status codes, which affects availability. To push an application to its breaking point, it’s not necessary to reach 100% CPU or memory usage. Applications can become slow and unresponsive, leading to client timeouts. Kubernetes health checks, specifically readiness probes, can also time out, and the application can be removed from the service pool.

For this test, failure means that availability drops, and the application can no longer handle requests within a reasonable time—in this case, 200 milliseconds.

## Reaching the Breaking Point

Alright, let’s push it to the end.

By the way, I also have a playlist on my channel with different benchmarks that you might find interesting.

At around 27,000 requests per second, the applications start to fail. So, I’d say the maximum sustainable load is about 26,000 requests per second before the response time degrades significantly and the application should be removed from the service pool.

Even if the latency varies between the three applications, they all started failing around the same time. Still, at this point, Actix had the lowest latency among all three frameworks.

## Analyzing the Final Performance Graphs

Now, let me show you the graphs for the entire test duration.

First, we have the requests per second graph. Next, the memory usage graph. You can see a spike in memory usage when the applications started slowing down and had to store more pending requests.

Then we have the CPU usage graph. As you can see, Rocket uses the most CPU. And Actix uses less CPU than Rocket and Axum.

Next is the availability graph. Although all applications started failing around the same time, we can see from this graph that Actix had higher availability, meaning it served more requests with lower latency. Next time, I’ll try reducing the load increments to see which one can handle more requests.

Finally, we have the client latency graph. Toward the end of the test, we see some spikes, but those aren’t the most important part of the test. Let’s focus only on the time when the applications were healthy. From this graph, we can see that Actix had the lowest latency and was the last to fail. Also, there was no CPU throttling because none of the applications reached 100% or even close.

## Conclusion and Call for Contributions

If you think you can improve the Rust code, any pull requests are welcome. Also, let me know what I should test next—maybe some programming frameworks or open-source projects. Thank you for watching, and I’ll see you in the next video.
